measures.label: New claims vs. a year ago
measures.footer: Initial claims rate (regular state UI, per covered job), 4-week average, % change vs. the same 4 weeks a year earlier. Year-on-year on unadjusted data: states' seasonal patterns differ and DOL publishes no state seasonal factors, so each week is compared with the same weeks a year earlier.

measures.label: New claims vs. normal
measures.footer: Initial claims rate, 4-week average, vs. 'normal': the median of the same weeks in the prior 3 years (weeks from March 2020 to June 2021 left out). Less sensitive than the year-ago comparison to one unusual year.

measures.label: Continuing claims rate
measures.footer: Continued weeks claimed (regular state UI) as a % of covered jobs, 4-week average, not seasonally adjusted; dated by the week of unemployment, so it runs a week behind new claims. Continuing-claims levels are not comparable across states: state benefit limits range from about 12 to 26 weeks, so in short-limit states UI claims end before unemployment does, and their continuing claims rates look low.

measures.label: Unemployment rate
measures.footer: BLS Local Area Unemployment Statistics via FRED ({ST}UR), seasonally adjusted, monthly.

measures.label: Unemployment vs. 12-month low (Sahm-style)
measures.footer: 3-month average of the state unemployment rate minus its lowest 3-month average of the previous 12 months, in percentage points: the Sahm rule applied to a state. No confirmation trigger is attached.

measures.label: Exhaustion rate (12-month)
measures.footer: Share of claimants who use up all their state benefits: 12-month average final payments ÷ 12-month average first payments 6 months earlier (DOL ETA 5159, our calculation).
